performers: String players of the United States Army Band
intro: The second movement of Ravel’s String Quartet in F major, Assez vif — Très rythmé, is a scherzo that opens with a dance in A minor played on plucked strings. Bowed melodies enter above the quick notes, and a muted cello leads into a slow middle section.

sections.label: A · Plucked strings in A minor
sections.mNote: Short plucked notes are followed by a high bowed melody.

sections.label: A′ · Mutes fitted, then cello melody
sections.mNote: All four players fit mutes before the slow middle.

sections.label: Dev · Short notes beneath the melody
sections.mNote: Pressez: pizzicato figures increase the tempo.

sections.label: A″ · The plucked dance returns
sections.mNote: Fortissimo, with A in the cello and leaps above.

sections.label: Coda · Soft fragments, final fortissimo chord
sections.mNote: The players pause before the last fortissimo chord.

relations.label: The plucked scherzo returns
relations.basis: The shortened A′ section restores the opening scherzo after the muted middle. The measured pair agrees with the return marked near 290 s; the identity and plucked scoring come from the form and listening notes, not from chroma. CENS diagonal mean 0.942, sustained 19 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 290 s (cache/form/ravel-quartet-scherzo.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening pizzicato, bars 1–4
cues.text: The two violins and viola begin pizzicato. The first violin leaps from A to E, then moves through C and D, and the cello enters a bar later. Ravel marks the movement très rythmé, with sharp accents placed across the beat.
cues.evidence: Quartet, movement II, bars 1–4; OpenScore String Quartets transcription by Bernhard 1964, from IMSLP 335585. https://github.com/OpenScore/StringQuartets/tree/main/scores/Ravel%2C_Maurice/String_Quartet_in_F_major
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: First violin melody over pizzicato
cues.text: The first violin plays high above the pizzicato accompaniment, pianissimo and bien chanté. Its line falls from E through D♯ to C♯, then rises again. Four bars later the viola takes up the melody.
cues.evidence: OpenScore transcription, movement II, bars 13–18: first violin E–D♯–C♯, pp bien chanté; viola bien chanté at bar 17.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Dedication to Fauré, 1903
cues.text: Ravel completed the quartet in April 1903 and dedicated it to Gabriel Fauré. He had lost his formal place at the Paris Conservatoire, but still attended Fauré’s composition class as an auditor.
cues.evidence: Stephen Walsh’s Chamber Music Society note gives the completion date, dedication and Conservatoire history. https://www.chambermusicsociety.org/about-the-music/compositions/ravel-string-quartet

cues.title: Lent, cello melody with mutes
cues.text: All four instruments are muted. At Lent (bar 89) the cello plays a high line marked p très expressif while the first violin rests. The viola takes over at bar 95, and the melody passes between the lower instruments before it returns to the violins.
cues.evidence: OpenScore transcription, movement II, bars 84–95: mute instructions, Lent at bar 89 with cello p très expressif, viola très expressif at bar 95.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: First performance, Paris, 1904
cues.text: The Heymann Quartet gave the première on 5 March 1904 at a Société nationale de musique concert in Paris. Ravel wrote no second quartet. Throughout the work the four players change between plucking, bowing and playing with mutes.
cues.evidence: Stephen Walsh, Chamber Music Society, gives the première and identifies Ravel’s sole quartet. Playing instructions are in the OpenScore transcription. https://www.chambermusicsociety.org/about-the-music/compositions/ravel-string-quartet

cues.title: First violin on the G string
cues.text: At bar 104 the first violin plays the figure again, low on its G string, mf expressive. It descends E♭–D♭–C, then rises through D♭ to E♭. The cello holds A♭ beneath it.
cues.evidence: OpenScore transcription, movement II, bar 104: first violin mf express., Corde IV, E♭–D♭–C–D♭–E♭; cello holds A♭.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Return of the pizzicato opening
cues.text: The opening dance returns fortissimo. The first violin leaps upwards through A and E while the cello moves between A, E and G. With the mutes off, all four players are plucking again.
cues.evidence: OpenScore transcription, movement II, bars 128–150: mutes removed, pizzicato restored in all four parts, ff at bar 150 with the returning A-minor figure.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Fermata and final chord
cues.text: The tempo slows (retenu), and soft pizzicato notes stop at a fermata over rests. At a Tempo the players play the final chord of A minor, fortissimo, and cut it short.
cues.evidence: OpenScore transcription, movement II, bars 197–198: retenu, p, pizzicato, fermata over rests, then a Tempo and ff A-minor chord.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: The cello leads into the Lent
transitions.from: A · Plucked strings in A minor
transitions.to: A′ · Mutes fitted, then cello melody
transitions.how: In bars 84–89 the upper strings leave an A minor chord and put on mutes while the cello alternates A and G♯ below them. After a bar of rest under a fermata in bar 88, the cello is muted too. Two flats enter the signature at Lent, and the cello begins a high melody while the first violin rests.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore transcription, movement II, bars 84–89: mute instructions, cello A–G♯, fermata in bar 88, two-flat signature and Lent.

transitions.title: Return of A minor at bar 150
transitions.from: Dev · Short notes beneath the melody
transitions.how: At Tempo 1 the original tempo returns and all four players remove their mutes. Pizzicato fragments lead to the return of the opening dance at bar 150. There, at fortissimo, the first violin leaps through A and E above the cello’s A–E–A figure, and the viola continues its quavers in groups of three.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore transcription, movement II, bars 128–150: Tempo 1, removal of mutes, restored pizzicato and the ff return at bar 150.

composer.epithet: Composer of a ballet built from two tunes and a snare drum, and of a suite of dances dedicated to his war dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery, and his mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He went back to the Basque coast many times. Spain appears often in his music, in the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera in the Rapsodie espagnole and the clocks of a Toledo clockmaker’s shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. André Gedalge gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and in January 1898 he entered the composition class of Fauré. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces he could not have played himself with comparable command.
